item.title: “Monks, then I thought: ‘This Dhamma I have attained is deep, hard to see, hard to realize, peaceful, sublime, beyond the scope of mere logic,…
item.description:
“Monks, then I thought: ‘This Dhamma I have attained is deep, hard to see, hard to realize, peaceful, sublime, beyond the scope of mere logic, subtle, to be understood only by the wise. But this generation delights in sensual pleasures, is devoted to sensual pleasures, is fond of sensual pleasures. For a generation that delights, is devoted, and is fond of sensual pleasures, it is hard to see this principle of specific conditionality (dependent origination); it is also hard to see the stilling of all formations, the relinquishment of all substrates, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna.’”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 26 – Ariyapariyesanāsutta
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “One who here has overcome sensual desires, Craving so hard to overcome in the world, Sorrowless, without longing, Has cut the stream, unbound. Dry up…
item.description:
“One who here has overcome sensual desires,
Craving so hard to overcome in the world,
Sorrowless, without longing,
Has cut the stream, unbound.

Dry up what is before,
Let there be nothing after —
If you grasp nothing in between,
You will live at peace.

For one who has no ‘mine’
In name-and-form at all,
Who grieves not for what is not,
Suffers no loss in the world.

For whom there is no ‘this is mine,’
Nor ‘this belongs to another,’
Finding nothing that is self,
He does not grieve at ‘I have nothing.’

Not harsh, not greedy,
Without desire, always the same —
When asked, I speak about
The benefit of the unshaken.

The one who has known without lust,
He has no inclinations —
Freed, not striving,
He sees security everywhere.

The sage does not speak
Of being equal, worse, or better —
Peaceful, without stinginess,
He neither takes nor rejects.” So spoke the Blessed One.

From: Sutta Nipāta 4.15
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “And what, monks, is dwelling heedfully? If one lives without restraint of the eye faculty, monks, his mind is defiled by forms cognizable by the…
item.description:
“And what, monks, is dwelling heedfully? If one lives without restraint of the eye faculty, monks, his mind is defiled by forms cognizable by the eye. For one with a defiled mind, there is no gladness. Without gladness, there is no rapture. Without rapture, there is no tranquility. Without tranquility, suffering remains. For one who is suffering, the mind does not become concentrated. When the mind is not concentrated, phenomena are not clearly seen. When phenomena are not clearly seen, he is called ‘one who dwells heedfully’ … the ear faculty … the nose faculty … the tongue faculty … the body faculty … If one lives without restraint of the mind faculty, his mind is defiled by phenomena cognizable by the mind. For one with a defiled mind, there is no gladness … he is called ‘one who dwells heedfully.’ Thus, monks, is dwelling heedfully.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.97

item.title: “Though one should rain down golden coins, One’s desires are not satisfied. Little sweetness, much bitterness — Knowing this, the wise one understands.” “The disciple…
item.description:
“Though one should rain down golden coins,
One’s desires are not satisfied.
Little sweetness, much bitterness —
Knowing this, the wise one understands.”

“The disciple of the Perfectly Enlightened One
Does not seek sensual pleasures,
Even heavenly ones —
He delights only in the destruction of craving.”

From: Dhammapada 179-196

item.title: “So too, monks, for one who wanders outside his own proper range, into the domain of others, Māra gains an opportunity, Māra gains an object.…
item.description:
“So too, monks, for one who wanders outside his own proper range, into the domain of others, Māra gains an opportunity, Māra gains an object. And what, monks, is not a monk’s proper range, but the domain of others? It is the five strands of sensual pleasure. What five? Forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, agreeable, pleasant, charming, connected with sensuality, enticing. Sounds … odors … tastes … touches cognizable by the body … desirable … enticing. This, monks, is not a monk’s proper range, but the domain of others. Monks, wander in your own proper range, your ancestral territory. When you wander in your own proper range, your ancestral territory, Māra does not gain an opportunity, does not gain an object. And what, monks, is a monk’s proper range, his ancestral territory? It is the four foundations of mindfulness. What four? Here, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body as a body, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and sorrow in the world; dwells contemplating feelings as feelings … mind as mind … phenomena as phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and sorrow in the world. This, monks, is a monk’s own proper range, his ancestral territory.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 47.6
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “And what, Aggivessana, is trained body and trained mind? Here, Aggivessana, a well-taught noble disciple experiences a pleasant feeling. Having felt that pleasant feeling, he…
item.description:
“And what, Aggivessana, is trained body and trained mind? Here, Aggivessana, a well-taught noble disciple experiences a pleasant feeling. Having felt that pleasant feeling, he does not lust after it, does not fall into lust for pleasure. If that pleasant feeling ceases, and due to its cessation, a painful feeling arises, he does not sorrow, grieve, lament, beat his breast, or become distraught. Aggivessana, that pleasant feeling arises for him but does not invade his mind and remain because the body is trained. That painful feeling arises for him but does not invade his mind and remain because the mind is trained. In this manner, for a person in whom either way — pleasant feeling arises and does not invade his mind because the body is trained, and painful feeling arises and does not invade his mind because the mind is trained — he is one with trained body and trained mind.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 36 – Mahāsaccakasutta

item.title: “The mind is fickle and restless, Hard to guard, hard to restrain. The wise make it straight, Like a fletcher straightens an arrow.” “Like a…
item.description:
“The mind is fickle and restless,
Hard to guard, hard to restrain.
The wise make it straight,
Like a fletcher straightens an arrow.”

“Like a fish thrown on dry ground,
Wrenched from its watery home,
This mind struggles and thrashes
To escape Māra’s grip.”

“Hard to hold, fickle,
It jumps where it wishes.
Good is it to tame the mind —
A tamed mind brings happiness.”

“The mind is hard to see, subtle,
It jumps where it wishes.
The wise guard the mind —
A guarded mind brings happiness.”

From: Dhammapada 33-43

item.title: Elder Nandaka: Foul is the thing! Full of foul smell and stench, Possessed by Māra, Oozing many streams — This body has nine streams, Always…
item.description:
Elder Nandaka:

Foul is the thing!
Full of foul smell and stench,
Possessed by Māra,
Oozing many streams —
This body has nine streams,
Always flowing.

Do not despise the ancients!
Do not insult the Tathāgata!
They do not long for the heavenly realm,
Let alone the human world.

The fool, without wisdom,
With evil intent, enveloped by delusion —
That one, full of lust,
Is caught in Māra’s snare.

Those who have escaped
Greed, hatred, and delusion —
They are not lustful,
The snare is cut, they are unbound.

From: Theragāthā 4.4
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Householder, there are forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, agreeable, pleasant, charming, connected with sensuality, enticing. If a monk delights in those forms,…
item.description:
“Householder, there are forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, agreeable, pleasant, charming, connected with sensuality, enticing. If a monk delights in those forms, praises them, and dwells with lust for them, depending on them, consciousness arises with clinging to them. Householder, a monk who has clinging does not attain complete Nibbāna … Households, there are tastes cognizable by the tongue … Householder, there are phenomena cognizable by the mind that are desirable … enticing. If a monk delights in those phenomena, praises them, and dwells with lust for them — because he delights, praises, and dwells with lust, depending on them, consciousness arises with clinging to them. Having clinging, householder, that monk does not attain Nibbāna. This, householder, is the cause, this is the reason why some beings here and now do not attain complete Nibbāna.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.124
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Monks, there are these three ways that sensual desire arises. What three? Sensual desire for present objects, delight in one’s own creations, and acceptance of…
item.description:
“Monks, there are these three ways that sensual desire arises. What three? Sensual desire for present objects, delight in one’s own creations, and acceptance of what is created by others. These, monks, are the three ways that sensual desire arises.

The gods who enjoy sense pleasures,
The gods of great power,
The gods who delight in creation,
And the gods who wield power over others —
Enjoying sense pleasures,
Here and there in various existences,
They do not go beyond the wandering.

Knowing this peril,
The wise should abandon all sensual desires,
Whether divine or human,
Here and in future states.

Those who have cut the stream
So hard to cross,
Who have broken the bond
To what is dear and beautiful,
Having made an end of suffering,
Without remainder,
Those noble ones who have seen,
The wise with knowledge,
Having rightly known the destruction of birth,
Do not go to renewed existence.”

From: Itivuttaka 95
📖 Read this sutta
